egg-omelet-or-scrambled-egg-with-meat-an.title: Egg omelet with meat and tomatoes, no added fat

content.title: About
content.content: Egg omelet with meat and tomatoes, no added fat is a dish made from eggs, lean meat (usually turkey or chicken) and fresh tomatoes, cooked without oil or other fats. It is prepared on a dry pan or in a microwave, preserving most nutrients.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Eggs are a complete protein source containing all essential amino acids.
Tomatoes are rich in lycopene, an antioxidant that becomes more bioavailable after heating.
Cooking without added fat reduces the calorie content by about 30 % compared with a traditional omelet.
Lean meat adds extra protein and iron without increasing saturated fat.
The dish can be quickly prepared in a microwave, saving time and energy.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Eggs and lean meat provide complete protein needed for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Rich in vitamins and minerals
items.content: Tomatoes supply vitamin C and potassium, while eggs provide vitamin D, B12 and selenium.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: The absence of added fat makes the dish suitable for low‑saturated‑fat diets.

items.title: Supports satiety
items.content: The combination of protein and fiber from tomatoes helps keep you full longer.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Lycopene from tomatoes and lutein from eggs help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to eggs and should avoid the dish.

items.title: Food safety
items.content: Eggs should be fully cooked to eliminate the risk of salmonella.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: If processed meat with added salt is used, monitor overall sodium intake.

items.title: Portion size
items.content: Large portions can increase total calories despite the lack of added fat.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the omelet hot, garnished with fresh herbs. It is convenient for a lunch box and pairs well with whole‑grain bread or a vegetable salad.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the cooked omelet in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2 days. Reheat in a microwave or dry pan without adding fat.

egg-omelet-or-scrambled-egg-with-meat-to.title: Egg omelet or scrambled egg with meat, tomatoes and dark‑green vegetables, no added fat

content.title: About
content.content: The dish consists of eggs, lean meat (such as chicken breast or turkey), fresh tomatoes and dark‑green vegetables (spinach, broccoli, green peas). It is prepared without added oil or fat, making it low‑calorie and protein‑rich.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Eggs provide a complete source of all essential amino acids.
Dark‑green vegetables are high in chlorophyll, which supports body detoxification.
Tomatoes contain lycopene – a powerful antioxidant that boosts immunity.
Lean meat adds additional heme iron, which is more readily absorbed.
The dish can be cooked on a dry pan or in a microwave using the natural juices of the ingredients.

items.title: High protein content
items.content: Eggs and meat supply the body with essential amino acids for tissue repair and muscle maintenance.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Eggs and meat provide vitamin B12, while tomatoes add vitamin B6, supporting nervous system function and metabolism.

items.title: Antioxidant protection
items.content: Lycopene from tomatoes and carotenoids from green vegetables help neutralize free radicals.

items.title: Bone support
items.content: Eggs contain vitamin D and phosphorus, and green vegetables provide calcium, together promoting bone health.

items.title: Low fat content
items.content: The absence of added fat makes the dish suitable for calorie‑restricted diets.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to egg white proteins.

items.title: Meat handling
items.content: Improperly cooked meat can harbor pathogenic bacteria; ensure it reaches a safe internal temperature.

items.title: Cholesterol content
items.content: Eggs contain cholesterol; people with high cholesterol should consume them in moderation.

items.title: Oxalates in green vegetables
items.content: Large amounts of spinach can increase oxalate load, which may affect those prone to kidney stones.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Beat the eggs, add diced meat, chopped tomatoes and finely sliced green vegetables. Pour the mixture onto a pre‑heated dry skillet, cook over medium heat, stirring until the eggs set. Season with salt, pepper, paprika or other herbs as desired.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the cooked dish in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours. Reheat using a microwave or a dry pan without adding oil.

egg-white-omelet-scrambled-or-fried-with.title: Egg white, omelet, scrambled, or fried, with cheese, meat, and vegetables

content.title: About
content.content: The dish consists of egg white prepared as an omelet, scrambled eggs, or fried, combined with cheese, meat, and vegetables. Egg white is a low‑calorie source of high‑quality protein, while cheese, meat, and vegetables add vitamins, minerals, and healthy fats.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Egg white is almost pure protein and contains virtually no fat or carbohydrates.
Cheese adds calcium and vitamin D, as well as a rich flavor and creamy texture.
Meat (e.g., ham or chicken) boosts iron and vitamin B12 content.
Vegetables (tomatoes, spinach, bell pepper) provide fiber, antioxidants, and vitamin C.
The dish cooks quickly and is popular in weight‑management diets.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Egg white supplies high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: Because it lacks yolk, the dish is relatively low in calories, making it suitable for weight control.

items.title: Calcium and vitamin D from cheese
items.content: These nutrients support bone health and immune function.

items.title: Iron and vitamin B12 from meat
items.content: Important for blood formation and nervous system health.

items.title: Antioxidants from vegetables
items.content: Vegetables provide vitamins A, C, and various phytochemicals that protect cells.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to egg white.

items.title: Sodium content in cheese and meat
items.content: Excessive sodium can raise blood pressure; choose low‑salt options.

items.title: Processed meat products
items.content: Sausages and ham may contain preservatives; lean fresh chicken is preferable.

content.title: How to Cook
content.content: Whisk the egg whites, add chopped vegetables, cheese, and pre‑cooked meat. Cook in a lightly oiled pan until desired consistency: omelet – firm, scrambled – soft, fried – golden. Serve hot.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the prepared dish in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2 days. Keep cheese and meat separate and observe their individual shelf lives.

content.title: About
content.content: Potato skins with cheese are baked potato halves, scooped out and filled with melted cheese, then baked until golden and crispy. They are popular as a snack or light meal, combining the mild taste of potato with savory cheese.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Potato skins are a staple in bars and fast‑food restaurants, often called “potato skins”.
Traditional filling uses cheddar cheese, but any meltable cheese works.
The dish originated in the United States in the 1970s and quickly became a favorite in sports bars.
For extra crunch, potatoes are usually brushed with oil before baking.
Leftover skins can be repurposed in soups or as a base for casseroles.

items.title: Potassium source
items.content: Potatoes are rich in potassium, which supports normal blood pressure and muscle function.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Potatoes contain vitamins B6 and B9, important for metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Calcium from cheese
items.content: Cheese adds calcium, essential for strong bones and teeth.

items.title: Protein
items.content: Cheese provides protein that helps with tissue repair and satiety.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: The potato skin supplies dietary fiber, beneficial for digestion.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: Cheese and oil make the dish calorie‑dense; portion control is advised.

items.title: Sodium levels
items.content: Cheese is often salty, which can increase sodium intake.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: People with lactose intolerance or dairy allergy should choose alternative cheeses.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: Large amounts of cheese and oil raise saturated fat content.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the skins hot, often with sour cream, guacamole, or barbecue sauce. They can be enjoyed as a standalone snack or added to salads.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked skins in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2 days. Reheat in the oven to restore crispness.

rice-brown-with-vegetables-and-gravy-fat.title: Brown Rice with Vegetables and Gravy, Fat Added

content.title: About
content.content: Brown rice with vegetables and gravy is a dish made from whole grain brown rice, a mix of vegetables (such as carrots, broccoli, bell pepper) and a flavorful gravy to which fat has been added for richer taste and texture.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Brown rice retains the bran and germ, providing more fiber and nutrients than white rice.
The vegetables add color, crunch, and vitamins A, C, and K.
Added fat helps absorb the fat‑soluble vitamins present in the vegetables.
Similar dishes are common in Asian cuisines, where gravies often include soy sauce, ginger, and garlic.
Brown rice has a lower glycemic index, making it a better choice for blood‑sugar control.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Fiber supports digestion, promotes satiety, and contributes to gut health.

items.title: Source of complex carbs
items.content: Provides sustained energy release, beneficial for active individuals.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals from vegetables
items.content: Vegetables contribute vitamin C, folate, potassium, and antioxidants that support immunity and heart health.

items.title: Fat aids nutrient absorption
items.content: Added fat improves absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) from the vegetables.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: Helps stabilize blood sugar levels, useful for pre‑diabetes and diabetes management.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: The added fat increases the dish’s energy density, so portion control is recommended.

items.title: Allergy to ingredients
items.content: Some gravies contain soy, nuts, or dairy, which can trigger allergic reactions.

items.title: Sodium level
items.content: Gravies are often salty; people with hypertension should opt for low‑sodium versions.

items.title: Food intolerances
items.content: If the gravy includes gluten, it may be unsuitable for those with celiac disease.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dish hot as a main meal or side. It pairs well with chicken, tofu, or fish. Garnish with fresh herbs, a squeeze of lemon, or toasted sesame seeds for extra flavor and texture.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. Reheat with a splash of water or broth to restore moisture. The dish can be frozen for up to 2 months, preferably in individual portions.

roll-hard-ns-as-to-major-flour.title: Roll, hard, NS as to major flour

content.title: About
content.content: Hard roll NS is a type of bakery product made from high‑quality wheat flour (grade 2358). It features a crisp crust, a light airy crumb, and a subtle nutty aroma thanks to natural sourdough fermentation.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Hard rolls are often used as the base for sandwiches and appetizers in cafés and cafeterias.
Flour grade 2358 has a high gluten content, providing excellent dough elasticity.
Traditionally the rolls are baked in steam ovens, which give them a characteristic moist interior.
In some regions the roll is called a “baton” or “loaf”, but the NS (non‑sieved) process retains the original flavor.
The hard crust allows the roll to stay fresh longer than softer bakery items.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: The roll provides slowly digestible carbs that help maintain steady energy levels.

items.title: Rich in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber supports digestion and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: B1, B2 and niacin aid carbohydrate metabolism and support the nervous system.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Iron, magnesium and phosphorus in the roll contribute to blood health and bone strength.

items.title: Low in added sugar
items.content: Absence of added sugars makes the roll suitable for low‑sugar diets.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: Contains gluten, so it is unsuitable for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Some recipes include salt; individuals monitoring sodium intake should take this into account.

items.title: Wheat allergy
items.content: May cause allergic reactions in individuals allergic to wheat.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Hard roll works well for sandwiches, toast, breadcrumbs for coating, and as a side for soups. Slice thinly, toast in a toaster, or use as a base for open‑face sandwiches.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the roll in a paper bag or cloth sack at room temperature, protected from direct light. For longer storage keep it in the refrigerator in an airtight container to prevent drying out.

tortellini-meat-filled-with-tomato-sauce.title: Canned Meat Tortellini in Tomato Sauce

content.title: About
content.content: Tortellini are small ring-shaped pasta filled with a seasoned meat blend of beef, pork, or a mixture of both. In the can they are immersed in a flavorful tomato sauce that preserves the taste and makes the dish ready to eat after heating.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Tortellini originate from Italy, where they are traditionally served with butter sauce or in broth.
Canned tortellini appeared in the mid‑20th century as a convenient way to store ready‑to‑eat meals without refrigeration.
The tomato sauce often includes herbs such as basil, oregano, and garlic for extra aroma.
A typical 300 g can contains roughly 30‑40 individual tortellini.
Canned tortellini are popular for camping and school lunches because of their long shelf life.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: The meat filling provides high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Source of iron
items.content: Red meat supplies heme iron, which is more readily absorbed by the body.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Tortellini contain B12, niacin, and riboflavin, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Lycopene in tomato sauce
items.content: Tomatoes are rich in lycopene, an antioxidant that may protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Quick energy source
items.content: Carbohydrates from the pasta provide fast‑acting energy, useful during physical activity.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Canned foods often contain a lot of salt, which can be problematic for people with hypertension.

items.title: Fat content
items.content: The meat filling can be relatively fatty, so those monitoring fat intake should watch portion size.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: The wheat‑based dough contains gluten, making the product unsuitable for individuals with celiac disease.

items.title: Preservatives
items.content: Some cans may contain food preservatives that can cause individual sensitivities.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Open the can, heat the contents in the microwave or on the stove until hot, stir, and serve. Tortellini can be added to soups, casseroles, or used as a quick pasta base.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the unopened can in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, keep the leftovers in a sealed container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days.
